But if you know how to add your own weight to the weight of nature, to double the Mercury and triple the sulfur, it will be finished more quickly into the good, thereafter into the better, and finally into the best; although there is only one visible sulfur and two Mercuries, they are of one root—neither crude nor over-cooked, yet purified and dissolved, if you have understood me.

    Indeed, there is no need to describe the matter of the Mercury of the Philosophers or the matter of their sulfur. No mortal has been able, nor will be able in the future, to describe it more openly and clearly than it has been described and named by the ancient Philosophers—unless one wishes to be an **anathema of the art** <note>original: "anathema artis"; a person cursed or excommunicated from the sacred knowledge of alchemy due to their betrayal of its secrets or their own foolishness</note>. For it is so commonly named that it is even held in no esteem; for this reason, seekers turn themselves toward other subtleties rather than remaining in the simplicity of nature. <summary>The author explains that alchemical success depends on balancing the weights of sulfur and mercury while following the simplicity of nature. He warns that the true matter of the Work is so common and clearly named by ancient masters that many seekers overlook it in favor of overly complex theories.</summary>
<keywords>Mercury of the Philosophers, sulfur, weights of nature, simplicity of nature, alchemical matter, ancient Philosophers</keywords>
